This Boston silversmith and engraver turned Patriot is best remembered for a 1775 midnight ride warning minutemen that British troops were on the march — who was he?
Paul Revere: American silversmith and military officer (1735–1818)
Ruling from Napata deep in Nubia, this Kushite king founded Egypt's Twenty-fifth Dynasty in the 8th century BC — who was he?
Piye: Ancient Kushite king and pharaoh.
Nicknamed after a judge was told to tremble before God's authority by their founder, members of this group call each other Friends and reject creeds and hierarchical structures — which movement?

According to the Hebrew Bible, this son of Solomon and grandson of David lost the ten northern tribes to a rebellion around 932 BCE, becoming the first king of the southern Kingdom of Judah — who is he?
Rehoboam: Biblical figure; first monarch of the Kingdom of Judah.
A human-rights lawyer who rode a wave of younger internet users into office, this man served as South Korea's ninth president from 2003 to 2008 — who is he?
Roh Moo-hyun: President of South Korea from 2003 to 2008. Roh's pre-presidential political career was focused on human rights advocacy for student activists in South Korea.

As students in 1930s Paris, this Syrian and Michel Aflaq cooked up a doctrine blending nationalism and socialism, then co-founded the Ba'ath Party — and decades later he was assassinated in Paris. Who is it?
This 44-day conflict in 2020 ended in an Azerbaijani victory over Armenia and the breakaway state of Artsakh, with the defeat sparking anti-government protests in Yerevan — what was it?
Second Nagorno-Karabakh War: Conflict between Armenia and Azerbaijan (2020)
The first Iranian ever to win the Nobel Peace Prize, this lawyer and former judge was honored in 2003 for her work on democracy and women's, children's and refugee rights — who is she?

Held every March in Austin, Texas, since 1987, this tech-film-music extravaganza also spun off an EDU conference and a London edition — what's this festival, often shortened to a three-letter abbreviation?
South by Southwest: American annual film and music festival.
He ruled an isolated pocket of Roman authority around Soissons long after the empire lost the region, until the Frankish king Clovis I defeated and killed him — who was this last Roman holdout?
Syagrius: 5th century Roman leader at Soissons.

Known in Hebrew as the Shoah, this World War II genocide killed roughly six million people — about two-thirds of Europe's Jewish population — through mass shootings and gas chambers at camps like Auschwitz-Birkenau. What is it?
The Holocaust: Genocide of European Jews by Nazi Germany.

Regarded as the founding father of his nation, this philosopher-turned-statesman served as its first president from 1918 to 1935 after campaigning across Europe for independence during World War I — who is he?
Tomáš Masaryk: Founding father of Czechoslovakia (1850–1937)

Going by VGE, this finance-minister-turned-president eked out a 1974 win over François Mitterrand with 50.8% of the vote, then liberalized French law on divorce, contraception, and abortion — who was he?
Valéry Giscard d'Estaing: President of France from 1974 to 1981.
Hitler called him one of his best field commanders and kept dispatching him to salvage collapsing fronts — which hard-driving German field marshal became famous as a master of defensive warfare?
Nicknamed the "Sailor King" for his Royal Navy youth, he was the last king of the House of Hanover and once spent two decades living with the actress Dorothea Jordan — who was he?
William IV: King of the United Kingdom from 1830 to 1837.
The first woman to hold her position, this French politician has led the National Assembly since June 2022 and briefly served as Minister of the Overseas before that — who is she?
Grand Duchess Maria Vladimirovna of Russia
His famous epithet is actually a pun on his name — "noble" plus "counsel" — and this King of the English took the throne after his half-brother Edward the Martyr was assassinated. Who was he?
Æthelred the Unready: King of England (r. 978–1013; 1014–1016)
Who among these was born first?
Henry Vaughan (born 1621) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these people was born first?
William Osler (born 1849) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four is the oldest?
COBOL (founded 1959) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four was founded earliest?
COBOL (founded 1959) is the earliest of the four. COBOL (Common Business-Oriented Language;) is a compiled English-like computer programming language designed for business use.
Which one below is best known as a physicist?
John Theophilus Desaguliers is a physicist. Desaguliers's most important patron was James Brydges, 1st Duke of Chandos.
Which of these four is a chemist?
Otto Hahn is a chemist. Otto Hahn (German: [ˈɔtoː ˈhaːn]; 8 March 1879 – 28 July 1968) was a German chemist who was a pioneer in the field of radiochemistry.
What is the atomic number of Californium?
Californium: Californium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Cf and atomic number 98.
In what year was Mohamed Atta born?
Mohamed Atta: In Hamburg, Atta attended prayers at the al-Quds Mosque where he met Marwan al-Shehhi, Ramzi bin al-Shibh, and Ziad Jarrah, with whom he formed the Hamburg cell.
In what year was Rakesh Sharma born?
Rakesh Sharma: Rakesh Sharma (born 13 January 1949) is an Indian cosmonaut and a pilot of the Indian Air Force.
In what year was Mikhail Lomonosov born?
Mikhail Lomonosov: One of the founders of modern geology, Lomonosov was also a poet and influenced the formation of the modern Russian literary language.
In what year did Hamish Harding die?
Hamish Harding: George Hamish Livingston Harding (24 June 1964 – 18 June 2023) was a British businessman, pilot and adventurer based in the United Arab Emirates (UAE).
In what year did Manmohan Singh die?
Manmohan Singh: A member of the Indian National Congress, Singh was the first and remains the only Sikh prime minister of India.
In what year was Plutonium discovered?
Plutonium: Plutonium is a chemical element; it has symbol Pu and atomic number 94.
In what year was Tungsten discovered?
Tungsten: Tungsten (also called wolfram) is a chemical element; it has symbol W (from German: Wolfram) and atomic number 74.
Ilyushin Il-96: Voronezh Aircraft Production Association. It is powered by four high-bypass Aviadvigatel PS-90 twin-spool turbofan engines.
In which country is Dassault Mirage 2000?
Dassault Mirage 2000: France. Work on what would become the Mirage 2000 originated with the "Delta 1000" project launched in 1972.
Who is credited with discovering Horologium?

Horologium (constellation): Nicolas Louis de Lacaille. It was first described by the French astronomer Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille in 1756 and visualized by him as a clock with a pendulum and a second hand.
Who is credited with discovering Hubble's law?
Hubble's law: Georges Lemaître. The Friedmann equations showed the universe might be expanding, and presented the expansion speed if that were the case.
Who is credited with discovering Eris?
Eris (dwarf planet): Michael E. Brown. Eris (minor-planet number 136199) is the most massive and second-largest known dwarf planet in the Solar System.
Hiding in coffee, fresh bread, and ripe fruit, this aldehyde is also what your liver makes when breaking down alcohol — and a prime culprit behind the morning-after hangover. What is it?
Acetaldehyde (IUPAC systematic name ethanal) is an organic chemical compound with the formula CH3CH=O.
This exaggerated immune reaction causes the body to mistake a harmless substance for a threat, triggering symptoms from a runny nose to a full anaphylactic reaction — what is it?
Allergy is an exaggerated immune response where the body mistakenly identifies an ordinarily harmless allergen as a threat.

Its name means 'unlike other shrimp.' Known best from the Burgess Shale, this extinct radiodont swam with body flaps and stared out through huge compound eyes packed with lenses — what was this stem-arthropod?

Anomalocaris (from Ancient Greek, meaning "anomalous", and, meaning "shrimp", with the intended meaning "unlike other shrimp") is an extinct genus of radiodont, an order of early-diverging stem-group marine arthropods.

Explicitly describing the relativity of motion and, by his own account, 23 years old in 499 CE, this figure is considered the first of the great mathematician-astronomers of classical Indian science — who is he?
Aryabhata (476-550 CE) was the first of the major mathematician-astronomers and early physicist from the classical age of Indian mathematics and Indian astronomy.

An Arctic and sub-Arctic cetacean, it is one of two living members of the family Monodontidae and is also known as the white whale (the only cetacean regularly occurring with this color) and the sea canary for its high-pitched calls. What is it?
Beluga whale (Delphinapterus leucas), is an Arctic and sub-Arctic cetacean.
Element 107, a synthetic transactinide whose most stable known isotope lasts barely 2.4 minutes, takes its name from a famous Danish physicist — what is it?
Bohrium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Bh and atomic number 107.
This general-purpose, multi-paradigm programming language was designed at Microsoft by Anders Hejlsberg and first widely released in 2000, later becoming an international standard. What is it?
C Sharp (programming language) is a general-purpose high-level programming language supporting multiple paradigms.
Belonging to the trumpet-vine family Bignoniaceae, this tree genus thrives across warm parts of North America, the Caribbean, and East Asia — what is it called?
Catalpa is a genus of flowering plants in the family Bignoniaceae, native to warm temperate and subtropical regions of North America, the Caribbean, and East Asia.

A long-term lung condition that makes breathing progressively harder due to damaged airways and lung tissue, this condition develops gradually and currently cannot be cured, though treatments and lifestyle changes help manage symptoms. What is this disease, commonly abbreviated?
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a long-term lung condition that makes it progressively harder to breathe.
This bird's name comes from the Quechua word 'kuntur,' and its California-dwelling relative was nearly wiped out by habitat loss — which giant vulture soars over the Andes?
Condor is the common name for two genera of New World vultures, each with one extant species.
Present in the cytoplasm of bacteria, archaea, and eukaryotic cells alike, this dynamic protein-filament network stabilizes tissue and enables cells to migrate — what is it?
Cytoskeleton is a complex, dynamic network of interlinking protein filaments present in the cytoplasm of all cells, including those of bacteria and archaea.

Derived from the wild rock dove and split into more than 350 distinct breeds, this domesticated bird was already being bred by Mesopotamians more than 5,000 years ago, according to cuneiform tablets — what's the bird?
Domestic pigeon (Columba livia "domestica" or Columba livia forma domestica) is a domesticated bird derived from the rock dove (Columba livia), of which it is also a subspecies.
Born in Pretoria and emigrating to Canada in 1989, this CEO of Tesla and SpaceX co-founded a web software company called Zip2 back in 1995 — who is he?
Elon Musk (born June 28, 1971) is a businessman and former public official who is the CEO and largest shareholder of Tesla and SpaceX.
This American businessman co-founded a disappearing-photo messaging app and became the world's youngest billionaire in 2015 — who is he?
Evan Spiegel (born June 4, 1990) is an American businessman who is the co-founder and CEO of Snap Inc.
This Caltech chemical engineer won the 2018 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for using 'directed evolution' to engineer enzymes, and later joined Alphabet's board — who is she?
Frances Arnold (born July 25, 1956) is an American chemical engineer and Nobel Laureate.
The last living species in an order that first appeared over 290 million years ago, this disease-resistant "living fossil" with fan-shaped leaves is also called the maidenhair tree — which is it?
Ginkgo biloba (-goh), also known as the maidenhair tree, and often misspelled "gingko" (see Etymology below) is a species of gymnosperm tree native to East Asia.
What protein filament, grown from follicles in the skin's dermis layer and composed mainly of alpha-keratin, is one of the defining characteristics of mammals?
Hair is a protein filament that grows from follicles found in the dermis.
Also called the ratel, this animal is Africa's largest land-dwelling mustelid, armed with remarkably loose skin that lets it twist around and bite back even when grabbed. What is it?
Honey badger (Mellivora capensis), also known as the ratel (or), is a mammal widely distributed across Africa, Southwest Asia, and the Indian subcontinent.
This Russian-American aviation pioneer, a trailblazer in both helicopters and fixed-wing aircraft, won the top prize at the 1912 Moscow Aviation Exhibition for one of his early designs — who is he?
Igor Sikorsky (25 May 1889 - 26 October 1972) was a Russian-American aviation pioneer in both helicopters and fixed-wing aircraft.
With brownish-grey fur and a pinkish-red face, this cold-hardy primate is known colloquially by a wintry nickname referencing the snow in its habitat — which species?
Japanese macaque (Macaca fuscata), also known as the snow monkey, is a terrestrial Old World monkey species that is native to Japan.
This Hungarian-American biochemist spent years pushing past skepticism to lay the groundwork for mRNA vaccines, winning a 2023 Nobel alongside Drew Weissman. Who is she?

Katalin Karikó (born 17 January 1955) is a Hungarian and American biochemist who specializes in ribonucleic acid (RNA)-mediated mechanisms, particularly in vitro-transcribed messenger RNA (mRNA) for protein replacement therapy.

A hybrid of the citron and the bitter orange believed to have originated in northeastern India around the 1st millennium BC, this small evergreen citrus tree bears a tart yellow fruit used worldwide — name the fruit?
Lemon (Citrus limon) is a species of small evergreen tree in the Citrus genus of the flowering plant family Rutaceae.
Named for a Dutch physicist, this six-parameter family of linear equations converts spacetime coordinates between reference frames moving at constant relative velocity — what is it?
Lorentz transformation are a six-parameter family of linear transformations from a coordinate frame in spacetime to another frame that moves at a constant velocity relative to the former.
Following fieldwork with the Omaha people and in Papua New Guinea and Bali, this anthropologist explored gender roles in her 1935 book Sex and Temperament in Three Primitive Societies — who is she?
Margaret Mead (December 16, 1901 - November 15, 1978) was an American cultural anthropologist, author and speaker, who appeared frequently in the mass media during the mid-twentieth century.
This field's founding body, the Bureau International des Poids et Mesures, grew out of an 1875 convention and eventually gave the world the International System of Units — what is this study called?
Metrology is the scientific study of measurement.
A demyelinating disease whose relapsing-remitting form shows up in about 85% of patients, it can cause double vision, muscle weakness, and loss of coordination — what is it?
Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an autoimmune disease where the immune system attacks myelin, the insulating cover of nerve cells in the human body, causing damage to one's own central nervous system.
Element 113, a synthetic and ferociously radioactive member of the periodic table, was confirmed by a team at Riken in Japan — what's its name?
Nihonium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Nh and atomic number 113.

Sitting in life's hierarchy between tissue and a full body system, this term describes a group of different tissues — like the epithelial and muscle layers of the gut wall — joined to serve one shared function. What is it?
Organ (biology) is a collection of tissues joined in a structural unit to serve a common function.
Which American biologist became famous for the controversial 1968 book 'The Population Bomb' and its dire warnings about population growth, famine, and resource depletion?

Paul R. Ehrlich (May 29, 1932 - March 13, 2026) was an American biologist, author, and environmentalist known for his predictions and warnings about the consequences of population growth, including famine and resource depletion.
With a musty odor like freshly cut hay, this toxic colorless gas is the double acyl-chloride cousin of carbonic acid, and it saw grim use as a chemical weapon in World War I. Name the compound?
Phosgene is an organic chemical compound with the formula COCl2.
Native to cool temperate regions of the Old World, which poplar species is commonly known as European or quaking aspen?
Populus tremula (commonly called aspen, common aspen, Eurasian aspen, European aspen, or quaking aspen) is a species of poplar native to cool temperate regions of the Old World.
Like a cosmic lighthouse, this highly magnetized, rapidly rotating neutron star is only visible from Earth when its beam of radiation sweeps directly toward us — what's the object?
Pulsar (pulsating star, on the model of quasar) is a highly magnetized rotating neutron star that emits beams of electromagnetic radiation out of its magnetic poles.
Which large Southern African dog breed, whose standard was drafted in 1922 in what's now Zimbabwe, descends from ridged hunting dogs of the Khoikhoi crossed with European breeds used to bay lions?
Rhodesian Ridgeback is a large dog breed originally bred in Southern Africa.
This Harvard political scientist argued in a 1993 theory that future conflict would erupt not between countries but between cultures — a 'clash of civilizations.' Who was he?
Samuel P. Huntington (April 18, 1927 - December 24, 2008) was an American political scientist, adviser, and academic.
The smallest of Japan's six native dog breeds, this small, alert hunting dog's name literally translates to 'brushwood dog,' reflecting its original job of flushing game — which breed?
Shiba Inu (Japanese) is a breed of hunting dog from Japan.

Extending from the base of the brainstem down to the lower back, this tubular bundle of nervous tissue is covered by the meninges and, together with the brain, makes up the central nervous system — name this structure?

Spinal cord is a long, thin, tubular structure made up of nervous tissue that extends from the medulla oblongata in the lower brainstem to the lumbar region of the vertebral column (backbone) of vertebrate animals.
A starchy tuber from the morning-glory family, often confused with yams in North America despite being only distantly related to them — what root vegetable is it?
Sweet potato (Ipomoea batatas) is a dicotyledonous plant in the morning glory family, Convolvulaceae.
This part of the lower limb sits between the hip and the knee, containing a single thick bone — the femur — that forms a ball-and-socket joint above and a hinge joint below — name the body part?
Thigh is the area between the hip (pelvis) and the knee.

Native only to New Zealand and resembling a lizard, this reptile is the sole surviving member of an order that was hugely diverse in the Mesozoic era, with fossils dating to the Middle Triassic — what's the animal?
Tuatara (Mori:; Sphenodon punctatus) is a species of reptile endemic to New Zealand.

First described by John Edward Gray in 1821, this family of small feliform mammals spans Africa, southern Europe, and Asia on both sides of the Wallace Line, and includes the genets — name the family?
Viverridae is a family of small to medium-sized feliform mammals, comprising 14 genera with 33 species.
Native from Panama to southern Canada, this plant genus of 50 species belongs to the asparagus family alongside the agaves — name the genus?
Yucca (YUK-) is both the scientific name and common name for a genus native to North America from Panama to southern Canada.
This protrusion in the neck, formed by the angle of the thyroid cartilage around the larynx, becomes more prominent in most men during puberty — what is it?
Adam's apple: Feature of the neck. The Adam's apple is the protrusion in the neck formed by the angle of the thyroid cartilage surrounding the larynx, typically visible in men and less so in women.

This organic functional group, structured R−CH=O and alternatively called a formyl group when isolated from its side chain, appears throughout biologically and technologically important chemicals — what is it?
Aldehyde: Organic compound containing the functional group R–CH=O.

Once sold as Elavil, this tricyclic antidepressant is now often a second-line choice — used as much for neuropathic pain, fibromyalgia, and migraines as for depression, thanks to its many side effects. Which drug?
Amitriptyline: Tricyclic antidepressant. Due to the frequency and prominence of side effects, amitriptyline is generally considered a second-line therapy for these indications.
Awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2008 for his AIDS-relief work on PEPFAR, this immunologist directed the U.S. allergy and infectious-disease institute from 1984 to 2022. Who is he?
Native to eastern North America's wet woods and swamps, this shrub genus produces bitter 'chokeberries' that reached Scandinavia and Russia by the eighteenth century — what genus is this?

Aronia: Genus of plants (chokeberries). Aronia is a genus of deciduous shrubs, the chokeberries, in the family Rosaceae native to eastern North America and most commonly found in wet woods and swamps.
Derived from a Greek word meaning 'that which is thought worthy,' which term denotes a statement accepted as true without proof, serving as a starting point for further reasoning?
Axiom: Statement that is taken to be true.
This common, noncancerous enlargement of a male gland can cause frequent urination and a weak stream; it isn't linked to poor hygiene, and there's no known cure. What's the condition?
Benign prostatic hyperplasia: Noncancerous increase in size of the prostate gland.
This small, fluid-filled pocket that forms in the skin's upper layers — usually from friction, burns, or infection — gets the name 'bleb' when it's especially tiny. What is it?
Blister: Small pocket of fluid within the upper layers of the skin. The word "blister" entered English in the 14th century.
Typically about two-thirds copper and one-third zinc, which prehistoric substitutional alloy differs from bronze, which swaps in tin instead of zinc?
Brass: Alloy of copper and zinc. Brass has long been popular for its bright, golden appearance and is used for drawer pulls and doorknobs.
This silvery-gold alkali metal has a melting point just above room temperature, making it one of only five elemental metals that go liquid in warm conditions — what is it?
Caesium: Chemical element with atomic number 55 (Cs)
This Cornell astronomer worked on the Mariner, Viking, and Voyager missions and won a Pulitzer for 'The Dragons of Eden' — who is this famed science communicator?
Carl Sagan: American scientist and science communicator (1934–1996)
Known commonly as tapeworms, this class of ribbon-like parasitic flatworms sheds egg-packed segments called proglottids — what is this class called?
Cestoda: Class of flatworms. Cestoda is a class of parasitic worms in the flatworm phylum (Platyhelminthes).
Known for an exceptionally loud song produced by rapid buckling of drum-like tymbals, some periodical members of this insect superfamily emerge en masse only every 13 or 17 years — which insect?
Cicada: Superfamily of insects. The cicadas are a superfamily, the Cicadoidea, of insects in the order Hemiptera (true bugs).
Also known as ubiquinone, this antioxidant cofactor helps mitochondria produce ATP and gets its name from ten isoprenyl units in its molecular tail — what is it?
Coenzyme Q10: Biochemical cofactor and antioxidant. Coenzyme Q (CoQ), also known as ubiquinone, is a naturally occurring biochemical cofactor (coenzyme) and an antioxidant produced by the human body.
A heart disease involving reduced blood flow to cardiac muscle due to buildup of plaque in heart arteries — the most common cardiovascular disease. What is it?
Coronary artery disease: Reduction of blood flow to the heart. Procedures such as percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) or coronary artery bypass surgery (CABG) may be used in severe disease.
This closed sac in the body, distinct from an abscess of pus, forms a shell of abnormal cells and may contain air, fluid, or semi-solid material — what is it, medically?
Cyst: Closed sac growth on the body. A cyst is a closed sac in the body, having a distinct envelope and division compared with the nearby tissue.

Found in many cough and cold medicines, this morphinan-class compound was approved by the FDA in 2022 as part of a rapid-acting antidepressant combo, but can act as a dissociative hallucinogen at high doses. What substance is it?
Dextromethorphan: Cough suppressant and dissociative drug.
Sold over the counter as Unisom and combined with vitamin B6 to ease morning sickness, this first-generation antihistamine is one of the world's most widely used sleep aids — which drug?
Doxylamine: First-generation antihistamine used as a short-term sedative and hypnotic (sleep aid)
Despite its name, this South American freshwater fish is actually a knifefish, not a true eel, and produces powerful discharges using specialized tissue — which species?
Electrophorus electricus: South American electric fish. It is considered as a freshwater teleost which contains an electrogenic tissue that produces electric discharges.
This flowering shrub in the family Erythroxylaceae is one of only two species whose leaves are cultivated to produce a notorious stimulant — which plant is it?
Erythroxylum coca: Species of flowering plant.
Sporting an orange-red breast rimmed in grey and brown upperparts, this small insect-eating songbird ranges from Western Siberia to North Africa — which bird?
European robin: Species of bird. It is found across Europe, as far east as Western Siberia, and as far south as North Africa.

This branch of Islamic scholarship interprets the Quran and sunnah through jurist reasoning, producing fatwas — while sharia itself is seen as unchanging, this human field is considered fallible. What is it called?
Fiqh: Islamic jurisprudence. Thus, whereas sharia is considered immutable and infallible by Muslims, fiqh is considered fallible and changeable.

Making up roughly 88% of all living amphibians, this short-bodied, tailless order gets its name from Ancient Greek for 'without tail' — and its warty-skinned members are casually dubbed toads. What is it?
Frog: Order of amphibians. The eggs then hatch into fully aquatic larvae called tadpoles, which have tails and internal gills.

A Belgian Catholic priest and physicist, he was first to argue that the recession of galaxies proves an expanding universe, and proposed a 'primeval atom' — the first version of the Big Bang theory. Who was he?
Georges Lemaître: Belgian scientist and Catholic priest (1894–1966)
This term describes the overall system of rules, processes, and power structures that steers decision-making within an organized group — what is it?
Governance: Processes of interacting with people and making decisions.
Occurring in any of the senses, this perception feels completely real despite the absence of any actual external stimulus — what is it?
Hallucination: Perception that only seems real.
This field of study focuses on the methodological principles of interpreting texts — especially biblical and philosophical writings — and is closely related to exegesis. What is it called?
Hermeneutics: The study of the methodological principles of interpretation. As necessary, hermeneutics may include the art of understanding and communication.
In Greek myth, this fragrant spring bulb sprang from the blood of a youth slain by a jealous west wind god who coveted his bond with Apollo — what flower is it?
Roche once used up to 90% of the world's crop of this star-shaped spice to manufacture the flu drug Tamiflu via shikimic acid — what is it?
Illicium verum: Star anise, an evergreen tree.
The largest tree fruit on Earth can hit 120 pounds and 35 inches long — a 'multiple fruit' made of thousands of individual flowers, with a single tree bearing hundreds a year. What is it?
This physician ran the Battle Creek Sanitarium — part spa, part hospital, part luxury hotel — where he treated the rich and poor alike and devised numerous nut and vegetable products — who is it?
Born in Kabul to a diplomat, this Afghan-American physician-turned-novelist wrote the bestselling 'The Kite Runner' before serving as a UNHCR goodwill ambassador — who is he?
Khaled Hosseini: Afghan-American novelist (born 1965). Hosseini's novels have spread awareness about Afghanistan's people and culture.
Known to some as Al-Kashi's theorem, this trigonometric rule relates a triangle's three side lengths to the cosine of one of its angles — what is it called?
Law of cosines: Generalization of Pythagorean theorem.
Sold under the brand name Vyvanse, this prodrug of dextroamphetamine treats ADHD and moderate-to-severe binge eating disorder, taking effect within about 90 minutes — which medication?
Lisdexamfetamine: Central nervous system stimulant prodrug.
Painlessly swollen lymph nodes, drenching night sweats, and unexplained weight loss point to this family of white-blood-cell cancers, split mainly into Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin types — what is it?
Lymphoma: Hematologic cancer that affects lymphocytes.
The second woman ever to win the Nobel Prize in Physics (after Marie Curie) shared the 1963 award for her discoveries about nuclear shell structure — who was she?
Triggered by falling progesterone, this regular discharge from the uterine lining signals that pregnancy hasn't occurred, and typically first arrives at menarche between ages 11 and 13 — what is it?
Menstruation: Periodic shedding of the uterine lining.
Known to NATO as 'Flogger,' this Soviet variable-sweep-wing fighter was the first in the country's air force to carry look-down/shoot-down radar, with over 5,000 built. Which aircraft?
Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-23: Soviet fighter-interceptor aircraft introduced in 1970.
Drawn from the latex of opium poppies, this naturally occurring opiate acts straight on the central nervous system to dull pain — but risks dependence and tolerance. What is it?
Morphine: Pain medication of the opiate family.
Sold as Aleve, this NSAID eases pain, fever, and menstrual cramps for up to twelve hours, and also comes in a more soluble sodium form — which drug?
Naproxen: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) used to treat pain.
Known informally as bedwetting, this involuntary condition rarely stems from a specific medical cause and is often treated with alarms or hormone therapy — what is it called medically?
Nocturnal enuresis: Involuntary urination while asleep.
This biological process turns a primary oocyte into an egg cell capable of developing once fertilized, beginning during embryonic development — what is it called?
Oogenesis: Egg cell production process. Oogenesis or ovogenesis is the differentiation of the ovum (egg cell) into a cell competent to further develop when fertilized.
Sold under the brand name Protonix, this proton-pump inhibitor treats ulcers and acid reflux but can, with long-term use, cause vitamin B12 deficiency and low magnesium — what is this drug?
This genus of fungi is responsible for both a groundbreaking antibiotic and the mold that ripens certain blue cheeses — which genus?
Whether captured chemically on light-sensitive film or electronically by an image sensor, this art is fundamentally the practice of recording light — what is it?
Photography: Art and practice of creating images by recording light.
With a half-life of just 138 days, this rare radioactive element occurs only in trace amounts within uranium ore and is chemically similar to selenium — what is it?
Polonium: Chemical element with atomic number 84 (Po)
Encompassing peaches, cherries, plums, and almonds, this genus of flowering trees and shrubs in the rose family produces stone fruits called drupes — which genus?
Prunus: Genus of trees and shrubs.
Botanically a kin of spinach rather than a true grass, this protein-rich Andean pseudocereal was first cultivated near Lake Titicaca thousands of years ago — what is it?
Quinoa: Edible plant in the family Amaranthaceae.
Aristotle called this ancient art 'the faculty of observing the available means of persuasion,' identifying logos, pathos, and ethos as its three key appeals — which discipline?
Rhetoric: Art of persuasion. It is one of the three ancient arts of discourse (trivium) of classical antiquity, along with grammar and logic/dialectic.

Named after the naturalist who first studied it and described in 1797, this extremely venomous South Asian snake is notorious for its excruciatingly painful bite and ranks among the region's 'Big Four' — what snake is it?
Russell's viper: Species of venomous snake. Russell's viper (Daboia russelii) is a species of highly venomous snake in the family Viperidae.
Driven by an empirical cycle of observation, hypothesis, testing, and conclusion, this systematic discipline splits into natural and social branches. What is it?
Science: Systematic endeavour to gain knowledge.
